column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (a short history and a list of products), little beyond the description

The article gives a reign of c. 539 - c. 525 BCE (Elayi's chronology); the entry says probably late 6th or early 5th century BCE. The reign years are left out; Elayi's placing is attributed to her. The article calls the stone amphibolite; the entry says black stone (not a contradiction).

The article says the Estates were founded in the Middle Ages by Arthur II, Duke of Brittany (who reigned in the early 14th century); the entry says they gathered from the fifteenth century. Arthur II's name and the founding date are left out; the third-estate innovation is given without naming him. Sévigné quotation paraphrased, not quoted.
The article says almost nothing of the Mississippian or Cherokee history named in the entry beyond the mounds site and the Hightower name in Cherokee records.
The article says only that a paper alleges Baring supplied the covering letter; worded as reportedly. The entry's figure of more than a thousand hangings is not in the article; not repeated.

Conflicts with the entry, left out: the article dates his second rebellion to 1072, says Alp Arslan forgave him and imprisoned him at Estakhr, and (after Ibn al-Balkhi) that he was killed in 1078 after trying to seize the fortress; it gives his reign as 1030-1078. The entry says he was put to death in the early 1070s (d. c. 1071). The article also says he had consolidated his rule in Fars by 1055 with Seljuk consent, while the entry has him seize Shiraz from the last Buyid in 1062; the article does not mention 1062. The 1355 end of the dynasty is the article's.

Some scholars (Beilis, from Masud ibn Namdar's panegyrics) place his activity as late as 1111; left out, as the entry dates him to the 11th century and the epigraphic date of 1096 is followed. The entry calls the line Kasranids; the article speaks of the Mazyadid policy. Neither name used.
The article gives his birth as between 1565 and 1568; the entry's c. 1565 is not contradicted, but no birth year is given.
The article's lead says the uprising lasted from May until November 1614; the body and the entry give 1612-1616. Not used.
The article's lead says the war lasted from 5 January (Zürich troops plundered Rheinau the day before the declaration); the declaration of 6 January is given.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the description
The article calls the ship USS Andrew Doria; the entry calls it a brig. Written simply as the Andrew Doria.

The article gives his death both as 16 March 1728 (O.S. 5 March 1727) and as 5/16 March 1728/9; no date is given in the text. A claim in 19th-century biographies that he was knighted is false according to his will; not mentioned.
The entry says he began the Barotseland mission in 1886; the article has the expedition leave in 1884 and Lewanika receive him in March 1886, which fits.

The article gives his birth as 1827 or 1828 and the marriage as 1853 or 1854; the entry's dates say 1827, so no birth year or marriage year is printed. The article says almost nothing of his work in the Cook Islands, which the entry already covers.
The article spells the county Werdenburg once; written Werdenberg, as in his mother's name. 'Lord of Prättigau and Davos' renders the document's 'zu Brettengow and Tafas'.

The article dates the declaration of war to 19 March 1858 'also reported as 22 March'; both are given. The article calls the first war Senekal's War and the third the Third Basotho War; the names are left out to keep the text short.

The entry says he was born Joaquim do Amor Divino Rabelo; the article says he was born Joaquim da Silva Rabelo and took the name Joaquim do Amor Divino Rabelo in religion. No birth name is printed. The article's lead calls him the main leader of the Pernambuco Revolt, while its body says no reference to his participation survives before its last weeks; the text follows the body. The article gives both 18 December 1824 and the 20th for his appearance before the commission; neither date is printed. The article has the Typhis appear from 1823 to 1824 (first issue 25 December 1823); the entry says that in 1824 the paper made him the voice of the Confederation, which is consistent.

The entry credits him with the palace and the Ludwigsplatz ensemble; the article lists the reconstruction of Saarbrücken Castle and the Ludwigskirche but does not name the Ludwigsplatz, so it is not mentioned.

The entry dates the crisis 1874–1875; the article says only 1874, so no year is printed for it. The article says the office ended on Wichaichan's death in 1885 and the crown prince was named in 1886, consistent with the entry.
The article does not mention Haakon the Good or the Frostating Court of Appeal named in the entry; neither is repeated here.

The article gives the adoption as 14 January 1639 O.S. (24 January 1639 N.S.) and also as 24 January 1639 [O.S. 14 January 1638]; the entry says January 1639, so no day is printed. The article also says the 14 January meeting drafted the Orders and they were adopted that day; the drafting date is not printed.

SKIPPED: The article is about 300 words and the entry already gives nearly all of it (planning, the French officers, the contract, the first ship, the damage of 1884); what is left would be under 150 words.

The entry calls the shrine one of the finest monuments of the Gampola period; the article says its main Buddha statue differs markedly from those of the Gampola period (1314–1415). The statue point is left out.

The article gives his death as c. 45 BC; the entry's dates read 1st century BCE, which agrees, but no death is told here. The article calls the Zela battle 'long and brutal' and the storm a 'tornado'; worded more plainly.

The entry dates the sale of Pesaro and Fossombrone to 1445; the article has Pesaro sold in 1444 and Fossombrone two years later. No year for the sales is printed. The entry's lordship of 1429 to 1445 is consistent with the article's 1429 accession.

The article writes that he "ethroned" Govinda Chandra; read as dethroned, since Govinda Chandra then asked Burma to reinstate him. The entry says he recovered the Kabaw valley for a time; the article does not mention it, so it is not repeated. The article says the British opened communications in 1823 and war was declared in March 1824; kept in that order as given.

The article says Raghunath Rao III died in 1838 but that the British accepted Gangadhar Rao only in 1843; both years are given as the article has them. The article places the adoption 'later that year' after the death of the first Damodar Rao in March 1852, yet also on the day before the Raja's death in November 1853; only the second is printed. The article praises his wisdom and taste in its own voice; reduced to what he did.

The article says Suklenmung built the city in 1540; the entry says he moved the court there around 1540. The founding year is left to the entry. The modern palace is said to have been rebuilt around 1752 under Rajeswar Singha, consistent with the entry's mid-eighteenth century.
The article does not name the battles of Leipheim, Böblingen and Königshofen given in the entry; they are not repeated.

The entry calls his Honduras post superintendent; the article calls it lieutenant governor. No title is printed for it. The Van Diemen's Land section of the article argues, partly in its own voice, that Arthur hid the mortality of the Aboriginal Establishment and points to an 'orchestrated diminution'; only the stated facts and Murray's warning are given here. The article says that in an 1816 article Arthur also praised the comforts of the enslaved in Honduras; left out for length.

The article says he became Comptroller of the Navy in November 1641 'for his service to King Charles II', which must be a slip for Charles I; no king is named. The entry dates the New Jersey grant to 1664 and its division to 1674; the article gives neither year.

The entry names Aldhelm 'of Malmesbury'; the article calls him Bishop of Sherborne. Both fit his career, but only the article's title is used. The entry dates him fl. c. 700 and says Ine fought him in 710; the article has him killed in 710 on the authority of John of Worcester, which is given as that chronicler's account.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance beyond the existing description (a few lines on the walls, the gate and the residents)

The article says the 1502 book probably describes events of the second half of the 14th century, while the entry says Interiano visited Circassia in the late fifteenth century; the dating of the journey is left out of the text. The article gives him as fl. 15th century; the entry's dates are 15th-16th century. No dates of life are given in the text.

The article gives his death as 1225 (c. 1150 - 1225); the entry's dates end in 1224. No year of death is given in the text. The article is short (about 270 words); the text keeps to what it adds to the description.

The entry calls him hereditary captain when he proclaimed the republic in 1921; the article says he inherited the leadership only on his father's death in 1925 and that his father had led the earlier rebellion for an independent Mirdita. The text says only that he led the republic and inherited the leadership in 1925, without naming him captain in 1921. The article says the republic was founded in alliance with Esadists; the entry speaks of Yugoslav backing. Neither detail repeated. Spelling of bajrak varies in the article (bjarak, bjrak); the standard bajrak is used.

The entry says he received the title of sebastokrator from the Despotate of Epirus; the article says he took the Byzantine title himself in 1386. The text does not say how he obtained it. The article gives Thopia's death as 1436 in the Aftermath section but as d. 1435 in the family list; no year of death is given in the text. The entry dates the taking of Gjirokastër to around 1386; the article places it shortly after his submission of 1385. The text gives no year for it.

The entry says the church was built between 1697 and 1700; the article says between 1698 and 1700. The text gives only the consecration date of 2 June 1700. The article lists Andreas Rudman as pastor from 1697 in one list and from 1698 in the cemetery list; left out. Membership and income figures of 2017-2024 left out as present-day statistics.

SKIPPED: different subject: the article is about the namesake general Gomes Freire de Andrade (1757-1817), executed in Lisbon in 1817, not the Count of Bobadela (1685-1763), governor of Rio de Janeiro

The entry mentions shipbuilding in the 19th century; the article does not, so it is not repeated. Recent planning items (sale of the Harbour Master's house, 2010 housing plans, cycle paths) left out as minor.
The article says the title was used until 1219, when the royal title replaced it; the entry says until Stefan the First-Crowned was crowned king in 1217. The text gives no year for the change.
The article gives the date as around 1450 BC in its lead and 1500-1450 BC from the 2016 pottery; the latter range is used, which includes the entry's c. 1450 BCE.

Spelt Gruffudd in the text, as the article spells him; the entry title spells Gruffydd. The entry gives d. 1286; the article says c. 1286 in its lead and later that he died some time between February 1286 and the end of 1287. No year of death is given in the text.

The entry calls him king of the Chionites; the article adds that he was probably of the Kidarites, which the text gives as probable. The entry's 73-day length of the siege is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article says the Crown terminated the charter in 1784 and the owners merged the company in 1785; the entry's dates end in 1785, so both are kept as the article gives them, the merger itself being in the description. The article's dates for the San Ignacio de Loyola contradict each other (a voyage of June 1733 and a last voyage and wreck in 1741); left out.

The entry says the code survives in a manuscript of about 1350; the article gives no date for Holm B 64, so the text names it without a date. The article's 'around 1220' is within the entry's 'probably in the thirteenth century'.
The article gives death as c. 1216; the entry's d. 1216 is kept by saying only 'later that year'.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 290 words, most of it repeating the existing description; the rest is a short list of passes and walls

The entry calls the theatre the German National Theatre; the article calls it the Hamburg National Theatre, which is used here. The Arons-Figal translation is described in the article as being produced; the text says it has been published online, with print planned, as the article reports.

The article gives his death as January 1367 (lead: died 1367); the entry gives d. 1366 and says Zhu founded the Ming two years later. The text gives no date of death and does not relate it to the founding of the Ming. The article's lead says Han Shantong was executed in 1355 and launched the uprising in 1351; the body says the rising of 28 May 1351 followed his arrest. The text follows the body.
The entry glosses Gaiwiio as 'Good Message'; the article as 'Good Word'. The text does not translate it.
The article dates the attempt to 1155 BC; the entry gives c. 1153 BCE. The text gives no year. The article spells the harem clerk both Pendua and Pentua; he is not named in the text.

The entry says she is venerated as a saint; the article says there was an unsuccessful attempt to promote her as a saint, that she was never venerated, attracted no cult and had no miracles attributed to her. Left out of the text. The entry says the community moved to Gandersheim in 856; the article says construction of the abbey began in 856 but was not completed in her lifetime and that she and her community lived in a temporary compound near Brunshausen. Left out. The article's 'largely forgotten by the 11th century' was left out as it bears on the veneration question.
The article says nothing of the Hevelli, Albert the Bear or the Margraviate; the history here is limited to what it gives (towns at the crossings, drainage, Fontane).

The article says he purchased the lordship of Plauen, Oelsnitz and Pausa in April 1549; the entry's 'recovered Plauen in 1547' was not repeated or contradicted (the 1547 occupation of Greiz is told). Both stand in sources: the entry gives 1547, the article's deeds date from 1549. Article gives Albrecht II Alcibiades and Albert Alcibiades; used Albert.
The article dates the Sobhuza biography 1978 in its text and 1970 in its list of publications; no year given in the text.

The entry dates the cutting away of the cross for a memorial to 1676; the article says the stone fell in a storm in 1674 and the cross was then removed for a memorial to Alexander Duff and his three wives. No year given for the fall or the memorial in the text. The entry describes the rider as a woman riding side-saddle; the article says she was long read as a female aristocrat and that modern scholarship identifies the figure as Christ or the Virgin Mary. Told as scholars' readings. The article places the base on display both at the John Ross Visitor Centre in Balintore and in Hilton of Cadboll village hall; the text says only 'in the village'.
The article's table of regnal dates was not included.

The entry says the abbey was refounded around 1180 under Domnall Mór O'Brien; the article says the original Cistercian monastery was founded in 1169 by King Donal O'Brien of Thomond. No foundation date given in the text. The article calls 21 January 1969 the founding's 500th anniversary, which fits neither 1169 nor 1180; the text says only 'an anniversary of the foundation'. The article does not mention the 15th-century rebuilding in the entry; nothing said of it.
SKIPPED: article of about 350 words, nearly all of it already in the entry's description
The article gives his father as Sithu II and elsewhere as Narapatisithu (the same king); the text uses 'his father'.

The entry says Northern Zhou conquered Northern Qi five years after 572; the article dates the fall to 578. No year given in the text. The entry says he became chancellor; the article does not use that title, and the point is not repeated.
SKIPPED: article of about 270 words; it also dates the Sudak campaign to 1223 (entry: around 1220) and names his son Alp Yürek as founder of the beylik (entry: Choban founded the dynasty)
The article says he became the largest landowner in the Punjab on inheriting his lands; the entry says his family was among the largest landowners. Not repeated.
The article says the Igbomina allied into the Ekitiparapo confederacy; the entry says some of their towns joined it. The text mentions only the revolt against Ibadan, not who joined.

The article gives Dharmapala Raksita's birth as both 1268 and 1269 and his accession as '1892' (evidently 1282); none of these is used. Rinchen Gyaltsen is called Phagpa's brother and his 'older half-brother' in different places; 'half-brother' used.
The article says the commission was formed by the Swiss government and established by the Swiss Parliament; the text does not name the body that set it up.

The article names the 1833 measure both as the Charter Act 1833 and the Government of India Act 1833, and gives an 'East India Company Act 1872 (13 Geo. 3)', evidently a slip for 1773; the text says only 'in 1833' and leaves the rest out.

Left out: the article's 'first indenture' terms laid down by Réunion on 18 January 1826, since the entry says the system began with the Atlas voyage of 1834. Left out: the lead's 'British Indian indentureship lasted until the 1920s'; the entry ends the system in 1917, as the article's own final-ban section does. Left out: the article's 'first ship, the Whitby, sailed ... 13 January 1838' to British Guiana, which sits awkwardly with the 1839 ban and the 1844 legalisation it gives for the same colony.

The agreement was signed on 12 December 2006; the entry dates the commission's work from 2007, so the text dates only the signing. Left out: the lead's present-tense remark that Morales 'is being investigated' over campaign financing.

The article dates the Elamite invasion to around 1823 BC and then says the great expansion started 'after these two brief incursions' around 1828 BC, which contradicts itself; the text gives neither of those two dates. The article does not mention Dadusha, whom the entry names as a son.

The article says the Hasanid sharifs were overthrown by the Saudis in 1924; the entry says the Sharifate lasted until 1925. The text gives no end date. The article also mentions sources dating his capture of Mecca to the whole period 951–961, which does not fit the entry's 960s; left out.
The article dates the cession of full ruling powers to 12 September 1949; the entry says he signed the merger agreement in August 1949. The text says only '1949'.

SKIPPED: too thin and partly about a namesake: the reign is one sentence, and most of the culture section rests on inscriptions dated 1027 and 1031 CE and on Someshvara's Manasollasa of 1129, a century before his reign of 1138-1151, so it cannot be told apart from Jagadekamalla I. The lead's claim that he still controlled the Hoysalas also sits against the entry's account of their growing independence.

The article dates the stone shell of the Manjakamiadana to 1869; the entry says the casing was completed in 1873. The text gives no year. The article gives his second mission as 1861-1875 in the lead and his South African years as 1835-1863; the entry says 1863. The text gives no year for his return. The article gives his birth as 1799 but his baptism as 6 January 1800; the entry has 1800. The text gives the baptism only.
The article says he settled in Bohemia after the archduke's death in 1662 but dates the purchases of Wittingau and Frauenberg to 1660 and 1661; the text gives the purchase years only.
Left out the article's placing of Mosega 'in Barotseland', which looks doubtful.

The article says he received the honorific patrikios 'in that year' (877) from Emperor Constantine VII, who was not born until 905; the text leaves the date and emperor of the title out. The article dates his death to 933 or 934; the entry has c. 933. The text says he died within the year after associating John II in 933.

The article says John made his peace with the king in the summer of 1476, losing the earldom of Ross; the entry dates the loss to 1475. The text gives 'the mid-1470s' for the summons and no year for the loss.
The article dates his joining Campbell's delegation to 1818 and his appointment as superintendent to 1822; the entry says he led the society in South Africa from 1819. The text gives neither year.
The article gives his time in parliament both as 42 years (1869-1910) and as over 50 years; the text gives no total.

The article says he is thought to have been born in Basel but that Montbéliard has also been suggested; the entry says Swiss-born, so the birthplace is left out. The article gives his date of death as 24 or 27 October 1824; left out (the entry gives only the year).

The article says he was born in Molo, Iloilo, and that on returning 'to Molo' he was elected Capitan del Pueblo, yet speaks of the people of Bago; the entry calls him 'from Bago'. Where he held the office is left vague.

The article dates the beheading to 'Good Friday, 17 May' 1546; left out as doubtful (Good Friday did not fall on 17 May) and not needed. The article says Hutten's party reached Neu-Augsburg (Coro), while other details place Carvajal at Tocuyo; the place of the clash is left vague.
The article gives his death as 15 July 1851 in its first line and 17 July 1851 later; the day is left out.
Nothing is known of Pardo after 1569, so the last section is 'Legacy'.

The article lists several datings: R. C. Majumdar and most historians 590–620; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri c. 600–620, revised to c. 590–620; Noboru Karashima c. 560–590 (or c. 590–620). The entry gives r. c. 560–590, so no figures for his reign are printed. The article says the Kalabhras were ended by the Chalukyas, Pandyas and Pallavas together in one place and by Simhavishnu and Kadungon elsewhere; the text follows the latter, as the entry does.

The entry dates the temple 'probably in the twelfth century'. The article says it is generally dated from the early 11th to about the mid-12th century: Dhaky and Meister 1020-1030 (Dhaky earlier 'around 1010'), Adam Hardy before 1087, Ajay Sinha c. 1075, and colonial scholars (Cousens, Campbell, after Meadows Taylor) a 12th-century rebuilding after Chola damage, which Hardy rejects. Because the article's datings mostly contradict the entry, no date of the temple is given.

The entry says he rebuilt Chiang Mai 'from 1796'. The article says he renovated the walls in 1795 and entered the city in February 1797. Neither year of the start of the rebuilding is printed; the ritual entry is told without its date. The article says Rama I consecrated him on 14 September 1802 in the lead and appointed him in December 1802 later; only the year is given.

The article contradicts itself and the entry on several points. Its lead says Khudabad was the Kalhora capital until 1768, when the capital moved to Hyderabad; its history says it remained the Talpur capital until the Indus flooded it in 1789. No year is given for the move. The article says Yar Muhammad captured Khudabad from the Panhwar around 1710, which implies an earlier town; the entry says it was founded by the Kalhora. The capture is left out. The article describes a present-day city of 75,000 with schools and a university campus; the entry calls it a ruined town. No 'The place today' section was written. The article's population, demography and education sections are left out. The article dates the Jamia Masjid to 1700-1718, before the capture around 1710; no date is given.

The entry says the poem was probably composed in the sixteenth century. The article gives Berg's case for c. 1550 or later (and says Berg was open to an earlier date), but also Damais's reading of the Kidung Rangga Lawe's chronogram as 1334, by which both poems may go back to the 14th century. Damais's view is left out so that the page does not contradict the entry's dating. The entry says King Linggabuana and his daughter were killed; in the poem the king is unnamed and the princess kills herself. The text tells the poem's own story.

The article spells the name Kim Hŏnch'ang; the entry's Kim Heonchang is used. The article says the rebellion followed King Aejang's killing by Kim Ŏnsŭng; it gives no date for that, and the link is left out as unclear.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words, most of it already in the entry's description

The article calls the war of 338 BCE the Third Sacred War (as its source, Smith's Dictionary of 1854-1857, does); it is now usually called the Fourth Sacred War, so the war is not named. The article is Smith's 19th-century dictionary text; the hellebore story is called romance there. 'Some ascribe to Solon' follows it.

The article dates the final assault to 752 in one place and the fall of the dynasty and Dantidurga's arrival at Vātāpi to 753 in another; the entry gives 753, so the final assault is told without its year.

The entry says Afrasiyab murdered Hasan in 1349; the article says Afrasiyab's two sons murdered him in his bath. Who did it is left unsaid. The entry names the victor as the sayyid Qawam al-Din Mar'ashi; the article calls him Mir-i Buzurg and does not give the other name. The article's name is used. The entry calls the Bavandid ruler Fakhr al-Dawla Hasan; the article calls him Hasan II.
The entry dates the Former Nine Years' War 1051-1062; the article says the victory over the Abe was achieved in 1063. The year of the victory is left out.

The entry says the Reddi kings ruled from Kondavidu until Vijayanagara took it around 1424 and that Krishnadevaraya captured it in 1515. The article gives the Reddi capital as 1328-1482 in one place and their rule as 1328-1428 in another, and dates Krishnadevaraya's capture to 1516. These dates are left out. The article gives the Golconda campaigns as 1531, 1536 and 1579 in one place and 1531, 1537 and 1579 in another, and credits the 1579 capture to Sultan Quli Qutb Shah; only the 1579 capture by the Qutb Shahis is given. The entry places the fort in Guntur district; the article says Palnadu district. No district is named. The article says efforts are in progress to make it a UNESCO World Heritage Site and describes planned restoration works; left out as not lasting facts.

The article gives Ptolemy's form of the name as Kolkhai; the entry says Greek writers knew it as Kolkhoi. Neither form is printed here. The source's 'chunk cutting factories' is read as chank (conch) shell cutting.
The entry says the abbey was founded by Louis the Pious for Benedict of Aniane; the article says Benedict founded it at Louis's suggestion. Worded so as to fit both.

The article dates Akitoye's escort to Badagry to March 1845, before the July 1845 rising it follows; no month given here. Idewu Ojulari's reign: the article gives 1819 to 1834/35; written 'to about 1834'.
The article dates Takkolam 'c. 949'; the entry says 949. The battle is not dated again here.
The entry dates his reign 'c. 1143–1172'; the article gives 1143–1172 without circa. No dates repeated here. The Taranga temple named in the entry is not in the excerpt given; not mentioned.
The article gives Shimazu control as 1603-1868 in one place and the medieval period as ending in 1609; no dates given here for Satsuma rule.
The article gives his death as 27 April 1867 in its lead and 24 April 1867 in its Death section; only the month is given here.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words and adds little beyond the entry (birth and death days, his Freiberg lodging, an honorary membership in 1893, Arthur Japin's 1997 novel)

SKIPPED: article is mostly lists (streams, religious buildings) and climate and area figures; its only history is the Arakan Army's capture of the town around 12 February 2024, too little for a longer text
The article ends the Reform War in December 1860, with Juárez back in Mexico City on 1 January 1861; the entry says 1858–1861. The war's end is not dated here.

SKIPPED: article has about 250 words; what it adds (the excavators, a second young woman possibly sacrificed, death in her mid twenties perhaps in childbirth, a face replica of 3 July 2017) would not fill 260 words without padding
The article says he was knighted K.C.B. in 1877 but lists K.C.S.I. in 1874 under honours; his knighthood is not mentioned here.

The article gives his death as 17 May 924; the entry gives the year only, and the date is not repeated here. He is called Prince of Qin from 924 in the article; not mentioned to avoid confusion with the entry's 'Prince of Qi'.
The article gives his birth as 268 BCE; not given here, as only his age of about 60 at meeting Liu Bang is reported in his own words.
The entry says Liu Yin's family was enriched by the southern trade; the article does not say so, and the point is not touched here.

The article dates the foundation to around 645; the entry says the seventh century. Not repeated. The article calls Lobbes 'the most important monastery in Belgium of the time'; written as 'the leading monastery of the region'.

The article gives his birth as 11 July 1730; the entry has c. 1730, so no day is given. The article says he fled in 1775 'and returned to England', yet was wounded off Sullivan's Island in 1776; the return to England is left out. The article has him serving in India 1752-1760 but promoted captain in August 1762; neither date given here.
The article calls Los Adaes the capital of Texas from 1721 (the first capital on its founding); the entry says 1729 to 1772. The start of its time as capital is left out.
SKIPPED: article is a short geographical note (about 300 words) on the river's branches, with nothing on the region's history; too little beyond the description
The article spells one envoy both Shen Fiji and Shen Yiji; he is left unnamed.

The article gives the army of the fourth campaign as 130,000 and, a few paragraphs later, as 150,000; neither figure is used. The article once dates the end of the fourth campaign to 1454, elsewhere 1449; the entry's 1449 is followed. Shan successors invaded Ava in 1527 in one passage and 1524-27 in a quoted one; 1527 used.
The article says the Morro held out 'another two months' after the attack of 1 July, yet dates Velasco's death to 31 July; the length of the defence is left unstated.
The entry gives his survey as A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200; the article gives ca. 1300 to the present (Macmillan, 1993). The title's dates are left out.
The article glosses the title as 'The Victory of Madurai' in its lead and 'The conquest of Madhura' later; the entry's 'Conquest of Madurai' is not repeated.

The article dates the city's founding to around 975 in its lead and says building began after 978, with Almanzor in residence by 981; the entry says from about 979. No founding year is given. The article's lead dates its destruction to 1011, its body to February 1009; the entry's 1009 is followed. A second basin in Marrakech is said to carry an inscription of 912-913, before the city existed; left out.

The entry calls him the fifth lord of Kaga; the article calls him the 4th daimyō of Kaga Domain and the 5th hereditary chieftain of the Kanazawa Maeda clan. His number in the line is left out.
